overview:
On 1 July 1569, after months of hard bargaining at Lublin, the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania converted a dynastic personal union into a single state with one elected monarch, one Sejm, and a common foreign policy — while each half kept its own army, treasury, laws and administration. The price Lithuania paid was steep: weeks before the deal was sealed, Sigismund II Augustus detached Podlachia, Volhynia, Bracław and Kiev and attached them to the Polish Crown, moving lands covering much of present-day Ukraine out of Lithuanian hands. Lithuanian magnates had walked out of the talks in March and returned only to salvage a federal arrangement rather than outright absorption. The joint parliament that emerged seated 114 Crown deputies against 48 from Lithuania, a ratio that tells you most of what you need to know about who led. At its height in the early seventeenth century the resulting state covered roughly a million square kilometres and held something like twelve million people — Poles, Lithuanians, Ruthenians, Germans, Armenians, Tatars, and the largest Jewish population in Europe.

What made the Commonwealth strange to its neighbours was not its size but its politics. Where most of Europe drifted toward absolutism, here the szlachta — a nobility far broader than the aristocracies to the west — elected their kings, bound them by contract, and defended a set of privileges they called Golden Liberty. In 1573, during the interregnum after the last Jagiellonian died, the Confederation of Warsaw committed the nobility to peaceful coexistence across confessions at the very moment France and the Empire were tearing themselves apart over religion; Norman Davies called its wording extraordinary for its time, and UNESCO added the act to its Memory of the World register in 2003. The tolerance was real but bounded: it protected noble consciences, not everyone's, and it sat alongside a rural economy in which the same nobles tightened serfdom on the peasantry whose grain paid for it. The same logic of consent produced the liberum veto, by which a single deputy could kill a session's entire work. In the seventeenth century the structure began to buckle under strain — the Cossack rising under Bohdan Khmelnytsky from 1648, which drew Muscovy into Ukraine; the Swedish invasion of 1655 remembered as the Deluge; and, on the other side of the ledger, John III Sobieski's relief of Vienna in 1683, which bought the Commonwealth the flattering and misleading title of bulwark of Christendom.

The eighteenth century turned weakness into dependency. Power drained from the Sejm to a handful of magnate families, and by the 1760s Russia treated a formally sovereign neighbour as a protectorate, managing its royal elections. In 1772 Russia, Prussia and Austria helped themselves to a first slice of territory. The reform generation answered on 3 May 1791 with a written constitution — drafted around Stanisław August Poniatowski by Ignacy Potocki, Hugo Kołłątaj and others, and pushed through a thinned Easter-recess chamber with barely half the deputies present — that abolished the liberum veto, made the throne hereditary, and brought townspeople and peasants within the protection of national law. It is generally reckoned the first modern codified constitution in Europe. It lasted about eighteen months. Conservative magnates formed the Targowica Confederation and invited Catherine II to intervene; Russian armies came in 1792, the king capitulated in July, a second partition followed in 1793, and Tadeusz Kościuszko's rising in 1794 was crushed. In 1795 the three powers divided what remained, and the Commonwealth vanished from the map for 123 years.
significance: For more than two centuries a very large European state ran on elected kingship, contractual limits on the monarch, and a constitutionally guaranteed religious peace — an alternative to absolutism that failed, and whose failure was long read backwards as proof that it was never viable. That reading was convenient for the powers that dismembered it, which is part of why it stuck. The Commonwealth also set the political geography that Eastern Europe is still arguing about: the transfer of Ukrainian lands in 1569, the Cossack revolt of 1648 and the Russian intervention it invited, and the partitions themselves are foundational events in the national histories of Poland, Lithuania, Ukraine, Belarus and Russia alike, told very differently in each. Its erasure in 1795 became the template case of a sovereign state extinguished by agreement among its neighbours, and the memory of the 3 May constitution — a reform passed too late and destroyed by force — has served ever since as a rallying point for Polish constitutional politics.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews plus retrieved pages on the Union of Lublin, the Confederation of Warsaw and the 3 May constitution; the dataset itself holds no events for this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date beyond what the text states. The surviving record is heavily weighted toward the szlachta, who wrote the laws, the diaries and the histories: peasants, urban populations and the Ruthenian and Jewish communities that made up much of the state appear mostly through taxation and litigation records. Casualty and population figures for the Deluge and the Cossack wars are estimates and disputed, and the whole eighteenth-century narrative of decline was shaped early by Russian, Prussian and Austrian writers who needed the partitions to look inevitable.
